kf: Infestation of the scalp hair by the louse ***Pediculus humanus capitis***.
Very common in children aged **4–14**; spread by **head-to-head contact** (lice crawl, they cannot jump or fly).
Diagnose only by finding a **live louse** with wet or dry **detection combing**; nits alone do not prove active infestation.
Options: **wet combing** (bug busting) or a physically acting product such as **dimeticone 4%**, repeated after 7 days.
Check all household members and treat only those with live lice; children need not miss school.

sub: Worldwide, all social groups; commonest in primary-school children, more often **girls** (longer hair, closer contact).
Direct head-to-head contact; sharing brushes or hats is a minor route.

aet: Risk factors: female sex, more children in the family, sharing beds, combs and hats.
Resistance to older insecticides (permethrin, malathion) is widespread, so physical or mechanical methods are preferred.
myths: **"Lice mean dirty hair"**: lice prefer clean or dirty hair equally.
**"Lice jump"**: they crawl from hair to hair.
**"Nits mean active lice"**: empty egg cases stay glued to hair for months.
patho_lead: The louse lives on the scalp and feeds on blood; itch is an **allergic reaction** to its saliva.

mech.t: Females lay up to 10 eggs a day, cemented to the hair shaft close to the scalp; they hatch in 7–10 days.
mech.cap: Louse and nits (eggs) glued close to the scalp on the hair shaft.

mech.t: Nymphs become adults in about 7–10 days; adults live about 30 days and die within 1–2 days off the head.
Lice feed on blood several times a day; sensitisation to saliva causes **itch after 4–6 weeks** of a first infestation.
Combing wet, conditioned hair with a fine-toothed comb is the most reliable way to find live lice.
mech.cap: Detection combing in sections from the scalp to the ends.

histo: Not relevant; diagnosis is by detection combing and seeing a live louse.
comp: Scalp **excoriations and dermatitis**; secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) and enlarged neck nodes.
prog: Curable; reinfestation from untreated contacts is common.
Treatment failure is usually due to incorrect use, resistance or reinfestation.
